title: Biosynthesis of Urea (Urea Cycle)
objectives: Understand the enzymatic reactions of the urea cycle
Identify the sources of urea atoms and cycle regulation
Explain the link between urea cycle and TCA cycle
Recognize congenital disorders of the urea cycle
Describe clinical management of urea cycle disorders

overview.title: Urea Cycle Overview
overview.content:
Urea Cycle Overview

Enzymatic cycle that converts toxic ammonia into non-toxic urea (NH2-CO-NH2). Occurs exclusively in liver, shared between mitochondria and cytosol.

  • Accounts for 90% of nitrogen compounds in urine
  • Substrate: Carbamoyl phosphate (from ammonia)

Atom Sources

  • C & O: Derived from CO2/HCO3-
  • First NH3: Glutamate, glutamine, or intestinal bacteria
  • Second NH3: Aspartate (from glutamate)

reactions.title: Urea Cycle Reactions
reactions.content:
Urea Cycle Reactions

1. Carbamoyl Phosphate Formation

  • Mitochondrial matrix
  • Catalyzed by CPS-1 (requires 2 ATP)
  • Activated by N-acetylglutamate

2. Citrulline Synthesis

  • Irreversible (OTC enzyme, X-linked)
  • Citrulline transported to cytosol

3. Argininosuccinate Formation

  • Citrulline + Aspartate + ATP
  • Irreversible (argininosuccinate synthetase)

4. Arginine & Fumarate Release

  • Reversible (argininosuccinase)
  • Fumarate enters TCA cycle

5. Urea Release

  • Irreversible (arginase, liver-specific)
  • Regenerates ornithine

regulation.title: Cycle Regulation
regulation.content:
Urea Cycle Regulation

Short-term

  • CPS-1 activated by N-acetylglutamate
  • N-acetylglutamate synthesis stimulated by arginine
  • Inhibited by acetylation (low ammonia)

Long-term

  • Enzyme induction after high protein meals
  • Enhanced during starvation

Energy Economy

  • Consumes 4 ATP per urea molecule
  • Produces 2 NADH (→ 5 ATP via ETC)
  • Net cost: -1 ATP (profitable cycle)

krebs_link.title: Link to TCA Cycle
krebs_link.content:
Krebs Bicycle

Urea cycle and citric acid cycle are interconnected:

  • Fumarate → malate (cytosolic fumarase)
  • Malate enters mitochondria via shuttle
  • OAA transaminated to aspartate
  • Aspartate returns to cytosol for urea cycle

disorders.title: Congenital Disorders
disorders.content:
Urea Cycle Disorders

Common Features

  • Hyperammonemia, encephalitis, respiratory alkalosis
  • Glutamine accumulation in fluids
  • Neurological symptoms: vomiting, ataxia, coma

1. CPS-1 Deficiency

  • Hyperammonemia type 1
  • Autosomal recessive

2. OTC Deficiency

  • Most common (X-linked)
  • Associated with orotic aciduria

3. Argininosuccinate Synthetase Deficiency

  • Citrullinemia (1-2g/day urinary excretion)

4. Arginase Deficiency

  • Late-onset symptoms (age 2-4 years)
  • Causes lysine-cystinuria

management.title: Clinical Management
management.content:
Management Strategies

Therapeutic Approaches

Dietary

  • Protein restriction + essential AA supplements
  • Frequent small meals
  • Arginine supplementation (except in arginase deficiency)

Pharmacological

  • Benzoate/phenylbutyrate: Alternative nitrogen excretion pathways
  • Carbamoylglutamate: For N-acetylglutamate deficiency

Surgical

  • Liver transplant for severe cases

Newborn Screening

  • Tandem mass spectrometry detects 40+ metabolic markers

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why is the urea cycle compartmentalized? +

A: The first two reactions occur in mitochondria where ammonia is generated, while subsequent reactions occur in cytosol. This separation allows efficient substrate channeling and prevents ammonia toxicity.

Q: How does OTC deficiency cause orotic aciduria? +

A: Accumulated carbamoyl phosphate spills over into pyrimidine synthesis pathway, leading to excessive orotic acid production that appears in urine.

Q: Why does arginine supplementation help most urea cycle disorders? +

A: Arginine splits into urea + ornithine, allowing partial urea cycle function. In defects before arginase, it enables excretion of nitrogen as argininosuccinate.
